sn12.66:1.7: _Sammasa_ is an unusual term in the suttas. The root is _mas_, to touch or rub. I’m reminded of the medical idea of self-examination, touching or rubbing your body to see if there’s a lump or pain.
sn12.66:3.6: “Attachment” is _upadhi_, which is both the things of the world to which we cling, and the inner clinging (see [snp1.2](), [mn105:28.2.]()). The Jains defined _upadhi_ similarly (Tattvārthasūtra 9.26). The dominant meaning in Sanskrit is “fraud”, which perhaps informs the Buddhist sense: the things we attach to give a false sense of security. Here it plays the role of “grasping” (_upādāna_).
sn12.66:13.10: Interpreting this passage is tricky; it seems corrupt. The drinks mentioned are _surā_ (beer), _dadhimaṇḍaka_ (buttermilk or whey), _maṭṭhaloṇikā_ (salted whey or sour cream, i.e. lassi), and _loṇasovīraka_ (salted infusion of fermented barley and herbs). These correspond with drinks mentioned, along with others, in the Cāraka Saṁhita as _surā_, _mastu_ (Hindi _maṭṭhā_), _dadhimaṇḍa_, and _sauvīraka_. These were fermented drinks used as purgatives, and some or all were also recreational liquors. Their consistent collation shows that _surā_ here should not be neglected, as it is in some translations, but it is  difficult to construe as stands. Read: _ayaṁ pipāsā surāpānīyena_. | _Loṇasovīraka_ is allowed as medicine ([pli-tv-bu-vb-pj3:5.33.14](), [pli-tv-kd6:16.3.1](); preparation methods are given in Suśruta Saṁhitā 1.44 and commentary to Pj 3). It probably originated in Sovīra ([dn19:36.6]()). Sanskrit just has _sauvīraka_ but Cāraka Saṁhita 3.1.18 says it can be drunk with salt; salted drinks are still popular in India. It was a great favorite of the women of Madra, who, it was said, would sooner part with husband or son than a drop of _sauvīraka_ (Mahābhārata 8.30). | The last phrase is corrupt, read _ahitāya dukkhāya_ following PTS and Bodhi.
